title: Ephemeral Safety Net: capacity routing and transient pool policy PRD
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Problem statement and goal: Large tenants occasionally trigger short, high-intensity spikes that are not well handled by existing reserved pools or burst mechanisms. Current approaches either over-provision (wasting committed capacity) or drop requests when out-of-reservation, resulting in customer-visible errors or large fallbacks to lower-quality model variants. The Ephemeral Safety Net (ESN) feature provides a lightweight, policy-driven transient capacity layer and routing rules that: 1) absorb short spikes without changing core reservation guarantees, 2) limit cross-tenant interference, and 3) provide observable, auditable fallbacks and cost accounting. This PRD defines scope, acceptance criteria, config surface, telemetry, and rollout plan for ESN on Redwood Dedicated.
scope: In-scope: control plane config for transient pool allocation and routing, worker-side admission/routing logic, console UX for enabling ESN per-reservation, telemetry and billing markers, canary rollout on a small set of tenants. Out-of-scope: wholesale scheduler rewrite, new GPU provisioning, long-term contract billing model changes.
requirements: 1) Control-plane API: new ephemeral_safety_net config attached to reservations with fields: enabled (bool), max_burst_seconds (int), budget_percent (0-100), priority_decay_ms (int), preemption_policy (string: gentle|aggressive|none), allowed_models (list of model ids). 2) Serving/runtime: when a reservation is saturated, eligible requests are routed to the ESN routing token if enabled and budget remains. ESN must enforce budget and per-tenant throttles. 3) Fallback behavior: if ESN exhausted, requests use configured fallback: queued, reject-with-429, or route-to-fallback-model. 4) Telemetry: emit markers (esn.used, esn.exhausted, esn.preempt) with reservation_id, tenant_id, token_count, and reason. 5) Cost accounting: usage must be attributable to reservation + esn bucket and appear in per-route cost breakdowns. 6) Console: toggle and sliders for budget_percent and max_burst_seconds; timeline showing ESN usage. 7) Safety guarantees: ESN must not decrease strict reservation guarantees for tenants with equal or higher priority. 8) RBAC: only admins and billing owners may enable ESN.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Functional: For a test reservation with ESN enabled (budget_percent=10, max_burst_seconds=30): a synthetic spike (3x normal QPS for 20s) is absorbed by ESN with no 5xxs and <=1% 429s when fallback configured to queue. 2) Isolation: An adjacent high-volume tenant with ESN disabled does not observe >1% increase in tail latency during the spike. 3) Budget enforcement: ESN usage stops when budget_percent exhausted and emits esn.exhausted; billing markers reflect ESN usage. 4) Preemption: When preemption_policy=gentle, lower priority queued requests are delayed instead of preempting active sessions; validate via integration test harness. 5) Console UX and API: config changes show in console within 15s and are applied to routing within 60s. 6) Telemetry: esn.* events appear in the telemetry pipeline and dashboards, and an alert fires if esn.exhausted rate > 5% over 10m for any reservation. 7) Security: feature passes security review and RBAC tests. 8) Rollout gating: pass canary with 5 tenants for 72 hours with defined SLOs (95th percentile latency within 10% of baseline, zero unexplained 500s).
metrics: Success metrics: a) Reduction in request failures (5xx/429) during short spikes by >=80% for canary tenants. b) ESN cost overhead ≤ 2% of total monthly Dedicated spend for tenants that enable it. c) No measurable degradation of reservation SLOs for neighbors (<1% change in 95th latency). d) Console adoption: at least 10 tenants enable ESN in first 60 days post-release. Telemetry thresholds: esn.used, esn.exhausted, preempt_count tracked per-reservation.
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (Design & Security) — 2 weeks: finalize config schema, threat model, and RBAC. Phase 1 (Canary) — 2 weeks: implement control-plane + serving changes; enable on 5 willing tenants; monitor for 72 hours. Phase 2 (Gradual) — 3 weeks: expand to 30 tenants, add console UI polish and billing markers. Phase 3 (General) — 2 weeks: full release with docs and SDK updates. Feature toggle: server-side flag esn:v1; default off for new reservations. Rollback plan: server flag off + immediate route revert to reservation-only behavior.
risks: 1) Cross-tenant impact if budgeting is incorrect — mitigated by conservative defaults and canary. 2) Billing complexity: ESN usage attribution must be correct to avoid disputes — require billing e2e tests. 3) Scheduling/latency path changes could regress tail latencies — require perf benchmarks and kernel selection validation. 4) Complexity in RBAC/UI may create support overhead.
open_questions: Should ESN budgets be billable as 'burst credits' or charged at discounted rate?
What default preemption_policy should apply for enterprise vs. standard tenants?
Do we allow reservation owners to delegate ESN enablement to sub-teams via RBAC?
How does ESN interact with autoscaling and pre-warmed workers?
